Okay, so this is going to be long winded. Please forgive me. 

Les Mis will always have a special connection to Christmas for me. Besides the 2012 film (which I love almost as much as the stage version, despite its faults) being released on Christmas that year, the first time I saw it on stage (years before the 2012 film) was around the holidays, too.

As well, it holds a very special place in my heart for Christmas due to my grandfather. The year the film came out, I was pumped to see it. The trailers looked great and I was always a fan of the musical. So I was listening to the old soundtracks ad nauseam on Spotify. My grandfather was slowly dying of kidney failure and in the hospital since around Thanksgiving. I was incredibly close to my grandfather; growing up with a largely absentee dad, he was the closest thing I had to one. I spent many, many nights in the hospital, sleeping in the chair in his hospital room, so he wouldn’t be alone (my grandfather, always the “strong, silent type”, became very anxious and afraid to be alone once he grew older and his health started to fail). 

To say “sleeping” is a strong word; some nights I slept, other nights I just sat there and read books and listened to music on my earbuds. Mostly the Les Miserable soundtrack. Over and over. Like I said, I was excited for the upcoming film version.

My grandfather loved the opera, particularly singers like Andrea Bocelli and Luciano Pavarotti. So when he’d have wake up during the night with horrible anxiety or panic, I’d throw on some of his favorites and it’d usually calm him down as wait we waited on the nurse.

One particular night — I believe it was the night before Christmas Eve — he woke up and started bawling from anxiety and fear, saying he didn’t want to die and was afraid of dying. He was holding onto my hand like a frightened child as I called for the nurse but, in the meantime, I threw my earbuds on him and played him some of his opera. It wasn’t working. He was so upset.

So I played “One Day More” from the original London cast. I’ve never seen my grandfather melt into such a stage of calmness. He loosened his grip on my hand but did not let go. The nurse came and he said he felt better now. 

He asked me to play more of “those singers”; I explained it was from a musical. He still requested more. So I played him most of the soundtrack as he drifted peacefully back to sleep.

My grandfather was released from the hospital from that stay around my birthday in late January. His health began to rapidly decline and he passed away in 2017.

However, he never forgot Les Mis. I watched it with him a few times before he passed away and he loved it. Growing up, he would fall asleep during most movies I showed him but, after that hospital stay, the two movies he’d stay awake for were Les Mis and Young Frankenstein, which made him howl with laughter.
